strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in LLM evaluation—benchmark contamination undermines progress measurement and wastes substantial benchmark creation effort
Core idea is elegant and intuitive: randomizing answers creates an unambiguous detection signal (Bayes accuracy ceiling) that contaminated models would exceed
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 benchmarks, 6+ model families, multiple training methodologies (pretraining, continual pretraining, model merging), with proper ablations
Theoretical analysis provided (Theorem 1, Corollary 1) with well-grounded binomial test for statistical significance testing
Practical flexibility: two strategies (concealment/disclosure) accommodate different use cases; works for private evaluation sets
Fair baseline comparison with canary string method; clearly identifies advantages (no log probability access, resistant to string removal, more stable)
Clear presentation with good motivation, intuitive figures (Figure 2), and comprehensive concrete examples
Demonstrates detection across diverse scenarios: base/instruct models, different scales, various benchmarks
weaknesses: Cannot be applied retroactively to existing benchmarks—a critical limitation since most contamination concerns involve published benchmarks; only works for new benchmarks at creation time
Limited scope: only applies to tasks with natural multiple correct answers (direct answer, multiple-choice); excludes generation, open-ended reasoning, and many specialized task types
Reduces benchmark utility: lowers Bayes accuracy, compressing dynamic range for detecting model improvements (Figure 3 shows non-phished benchmarks better capture performance differences)
Method fails for cross-lingual contamination detection when reasoning is required (Figure 6b)—only detects on European languages without reasoning for GSM8K, contradicting broad applicability claims

Restrictive theoretical assumptions (A1-A4) primarily developed for multiple-choice; direct answer tasks and reasoning tasks lack equivalent analysis; Assumption (A4) about random option permutation may not hold in practice

Detection mechanism assumes models memorize specific randomized answers rather than learning better generalizations or distributions over valid answers—doesn't account for implicit contamination or paraphrasing

Incomplete baseline comparison: only compares with canary string method; missing comparisons with other detection approaches (probability-based: Golchin & Surdeanu 2024, Oren et al. 2024; internals-based: Shi et al. 2024)
Pretraining from scratch experiment uses very small benchmark subsamples (max 1024 vs. full size)—unclear if results scale; GPT-2 XL also limits generalizability to modern models
Statistical analysis incomplete: no Type I/II error analysis for binomial test; upper bound 1/L (Corollary 1) can be loose; substantial standard deviations (Table 1: ±3-4%) lack significance testing
Practical barriers to adoption: requires benchmark creators to explicitly use this method; no code release mentioned; creates modified benchmarks that community must adopt
Trade-off between detection power and benchmark utility not thoroughly explored—very low Bayes accuracy (10%) loses benchmark utility without proportional detection improvement (Figure 6a)
No discussion of circumvention strategies by sophisticated adversaries aware of the method; potential for malicious benchmark creators to use non-uniform distributions to hide contamination

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem of LLM benchmark contamination with clear practical motivation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 8 benchmarks, 6+ model families, and multiple training scenarios
Demonstrates broad applicability to different task types and evaluation settings (public/private)
Provides comparison with baseline method (canary strings) and identifies advantages
Includes formal theoretical analysis with Theorem 1 characterizing score relationships
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: straightforward application of existing Bayes error concepts without clear distinction from prior work
Theoretical assumptions (A1-A4) are strong and unjustified; no analysis of violation consequences. Assumption A4 especially problematic given models' positional biases
All experiments use controlled contamination with exact phished data—unrealistic. Real contamination is partial, paraphrased, unintentional. No evaluation on naturally contaminated data
Method requires models memorize exact randomized answers; no evidence this holds across contamination types. Models may learn invariant task structure instead
Limited applicability: restricted to tasks with multiple correct answers; fails for generation, open-ended, and unique-solution tasks
Insufficient trade-off analysis: reducing Bayes accuracy degrades benchmark's ability to track improvements. No principled guidance for choosing K
Statistical concerns: assumes question independence (likely violated), no multiple testing correction, small samples for some benchmarks
Figure 6b shows method fails to detect cross-lingual contamination for reasoning tasks, contradicting claims about 'deep contamination' detection
Incomplete baselines: only compares to canary strings; missing other contamination detection methods from literature
Reproducibility issues: no code availability, vague randomization procedures for direct answer tasks, only 3 random seeds

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem in LLM benchmark publishing with practical importance and clear motivation

Elegant and simple core idea with solid theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 provides an interpretable affine relationship between phished and original scores, demonstrating performance rankings are preserved

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8+ benchmarks, multiple model families (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek), and diverse training scenarios (pretraining, continual pretraining, model merging, cross-lingual, private evaluation)
Consistent and reliable contamination detection across all tested configurations and Bayes accuracy levels (10%-50%), outperforming canary string baseline with more stable results
Practical flexibility demonstrated through two implementation strategies (concealment and disclosure-allowed) with concrete usable examples
Black-box compatible and resistant to malicious canary string removal, making it applicable in real-world deployment scenarios
Well-executed presentation with clear motivation, good visualizations, and reproducible experiments (dataset URLs, concrete examples, multiple random seeds)
weaknesses: Limited applicability restricted to direct-answer and multiple-choice tasks; cannot handle open-ended generation, subjective evaluation, or tasks without clear alternative correct answers, limiting utility for many modern LLM applications

Strong theoretical assumptions (A1-A4) insufficiently validated empirically; A2 (independence assumption) and A4 (uniform random permutation) may not hold in practice, with unclear consequences for assumption violations

Incomplete guidance on practical design choices: no principled framework for selecting Bayes accuracy levels or determining K(x) for different benchmarks despite the significant accuracy-detection trade-off demonstrated in Figure 6a
Insufficient analysis of edge cases: GSM8K-with-reasoning fails for non-English languages without adequate investigation; no discussion of handling tasks with subjective or ambiguous correct answers

Statistical testing details not fully justified: no discussion of independence assumptions in binomial test, lack of multiple testing corrections despite simultaneous benchmark testing, and choice of α=0.05 unjustified

Experimental design limitations: contamination simulated through controlled pretraining rather than natural contamination; gap between theory (multiple-choice with modular arithmetic) and diverse experimental formats not well addressed

Practical implementation challenges underexplored: limited systematic guidance for generating alternative answers that maintain difficulty and validity, particularly for mathematical and factual QA tasks

Incomplete comparison with related work: limited comparison to other contamination detection methods (Oren et al. 2024, Shi et al. 2024 mentioned but not compared); potential for hybrid approaches combining methods not explored

strengths: Addresses timely problem: benchmark contamination with well-motivated statistics on rising benchmark creation costs
Solid empirical validation across 10 benchmarks, multiple model families, and diverse contamination scenarios including cross-lingual transfer
Theoretically grounded approach with Theorem 1-2 relating phished/original scores and binomial test based on Kerlin-Rubin theorem
Practical advantages: works on black-box models, stable detection across training epochs, resilient to malicious canary removal
Maintains reasonable ranking correlation (avg Kendall's τ=0.96) for comparing model progress
Clear presentation with compelling motivation and effective visualizations
Honest discussion of limitations and applicability restrictions
weaknesses: Theoretical results restricted to multiple-choice questions; direct-answer tasks rely entirely on empirical validation without guarantees
Variance of phished estimator increases 2-3x (GSM8K: 0.011→0.027, MMLU: 0.003→0.012), reducing benchmark informativeness for fine-grained model discrimination
Reverse engineering succeeds on several benchmarks (GSM8K 95.95%, GPQA 47.87%), undermining security claims; no systematic evaluation of sophisticated attacks
Deep contamination detection fails for non-English reasoning tasks (Figure 6b) with incomplete explanation and no proposed solution
Method applicability limited to ~30% of benchmarks (direct-answer, multiple-choice); excludes open-ended generation, code synthesis, image understanding
Core assumptions require model compliance with randomization instructions; no principled verification method and malicious developers can remove instructions
Key design choices lack justification and ablation: why K=2, uniform shift distribution, α=5% significance level
Model ranking preservation claims insufficiently qualified: variation in Kendall's τ (GPQA 0.35, BoolQ 0.60) masks failure modes
Bayes accuracy estimation assumes knowledge of all logically correct answers, which is subjective and difficult in practice; no guidance for creating answer sets
Code not released; reproducibility concerns with implementation details scattered across appendices

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem of benchmark contamination in LLMs with practical relevance
Solid theoretical framework grounding detection in Bayes error and uniformly most powerful testing
Comprehensive experimental validation across 10+ benchmarks, multiple model families, and diverse training paradigms
Transparent presentation of limitations and honest discussion of failure modes (e.g., deep contamination)
Flexible approach with both concealment and disclosure-allowed strategies
weaknesses: Severely limited applicability: Method only works for multiple-choice and direct-answer tasks, excluding open-ended generation, code, essays—a major portion of modern LLM evaluation
Critical failure on deep contamination: Figure 6b shows zero detection on GSM8K reasoning tasks in non-English languages; inadequately explained and problematic for realistic scenarios

Reverse engineering vulnerability: Table 3 shows near-original performance (95.95% vs 94.12%) when reverse engineering the randomization rule; defense relies on obscurity rather than fundamental security
Models fail to follow randomization instructions without reasoning prompts (Section B.2, Table 4), introducing brittle engineering requirements and inconsistent compliance across architectures
Restrictive theoretical assumptions (A1-A4) that may not hold for diverse models; no analysis of robustness to assumption violations

Insufficient statistical rigor: No ROC curves, false positive/negative analysis, or systematic study of detection sensitivity vs. contamination levels; binomial test uses loose upper bounds without power analysis
Limited conceptual novelty: Randomizing labels to reduce classifier ceiling is standard practice; incremental advance over canary strings without principled justification
Artificial experimental contamination scenarios (subsampled benchmarks in pretraining) don't reflect realistic large-scale data leakage
Dismissed but significant variance penalty: 1.5-2.4× standard deviation increase could impact model ranking, especially for close comparisons and saturated benchmarks
Incomplete baseline comparison: Canary string analysis is superficial; no engagement with differential privacy, watermarking, or other principled label obfuscation approaches

Missing critical analysis: No discussion of multi-organization coordination challenges, malicious actors with benchmark access, or clear guidance on when practitioners should adopt this vs. alternatives

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem in LLM evaluation with practical relevance to benchmark design
Solid theoretical foundation with formal analysis (Theorems 1-2) and uniformly most powerful binomial test justified by Kerlin-Rubin theorem
Comprehensive experimental validation: 10 benchmarks, 11+ models, multiple training regimes, diverse contamination scenarios, strong correlation (τ=0.96) between phished and non-phished performance
Elegant and simple solution that doesn't require access to model internals or log probabilities, enabling black-box evaluation
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, effective examples, thorough appendix, and honest discussion of limitations including failure cases
Flexible methodology applicable to multiple task types with both concealment and disclosure-allowed strategies
Robust to prompt variations and demonstrates reliability across different model architectures and sizes
weaknesses: Reverse engineering attack shows concerning success rates (GSM8K: 95.95%, Table 3), contradicting claims that answers are effectively hidden, particularly problematic for quantitative reasoning tasks
Cross-lingual contamination detection fails for reasoning-based tasks (Figure 6b), revealing important applicability gap for multilingual evaluation

Strong assumptions in Theorem 1 (particularly A2 independence and A3 model behavior) lack empirical validation that they hold in practice; independence assumption could be violated if models learn randomization patterns
Variance increases substantially in phished estimates (2.5× for GSM8K per Theorem 2), which could impact model ranking despite authors' 'modest' characterization
Limited to specific task types (direct answer, multiple-choice, binary); difficult to apply to open-ended generation, complex reasoning chains, or coding
Weak baseline comparison limited to canary strings; missing comparisons to other contamination detection methods; no analysis of whether canary failure reflects implementation issue
Validation uses only controlled contamination; lacks real-world contamination case studies
Methodologically incremental—core idea of randomizing answers is straightforward; Bayes accuracy concept borrowed from classical ML literature
